General Assembly
JEN-er-al uh-SEM-blee
proper noun / noun
From Latin generalis, “of the whole,” and assembly, a gathering called together; the highest court of Presbyterian polity.

Biblical Definition

In Presbyterian polity the General Assembly is the highest of the church courts, gathering ministers and ruling elders from the whole communion to deliberate, to judge appeals, and to maintain the peace and purity of the church. It rises above the session, the presbytery, and the synod, and is the visible bond of a connectional church, after the pattern the Presbyterian reads in the council at Jerusalem, where the apostles and elders came together to consider a weighty matter, and decreed what seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to them (Act 15:6, 28). The Scriptures honour the gathering of the elders to take counsel and the doing of all things decently and in order (1Co 14:40), and the dictionary honours the gravity and good order of the Presbyterian courts. Yet the phrase rises higher still, for the Holy Ghost speaks of a heavenly General Assembly: the believer is come “unto the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven” (Heb 12:23), gathered unto mount Sion, the city of the living God. The earthly courts are but shadows of that great congregation of the redeemed. Here the dictionary speaks plainly of its own confession: the 1689 London Baptist Confession holds that government is committed to each local congregation under its own elders (LBCF 26), not to a hierarchy of courts; yet it esteems the brotherly counsel of the churches together, and honours all that is decent, orderly, and Scriptural in the Presbyterian way.

Webster 1828 Definition

The highest court of Presbyterian polity; and the heavenly assembly and church of the firstborn written in heaven (Heb 12:23).

GENERAL ASSEMBLY, the highest court in Presbyterian polity.

It gathers ministers and ruling elders from the whole communion.

It rises above session, presbytery, and synod as the bond of a connectional church.

The Baptist holds instead to local-church congregational government (LBCF 26).

Scripture names a heavenly “general assembly and church of the firstborn” (Heb 12:23).

Key Scripture

Heb 12:22 — "But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels,"

Heb 12:23 — "To the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven, and to God the Judge of all, and to the spirits of just men made perfect,"

Act 15:6 — "And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter."

1Co 14:40 — "Let all things be done decently and in order."

Modern Corruption

Honoured for its order and counsel, the Presbyterian court differs from the Baptist's congregational government, which the dictionary confesses (LBCF 26).

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter here is not a postmodern grievance but an honest difference of polity among brethren who hold one gospel. The Presbyterian General Assembly is a grave and orderly court, and the dictionary honours its care to do all things decently and in order, after the example of the apostles and elders gathered at Jerusalem. The principle to recover is that Christ governs His church by appointed officers and orderly counsel, not by the whim of the crowd nor the will of one prelate.

Yet the dictionary confesses the 1689 London Baptist position: that the Lord Jesus has given power and authority to each particular congregation, gathered according to His mind, to carry on its own government under its own elders, and that the highest court on earth is the assembled local church (LBCF 26). This is not named a corruption but an honest difference from the Presbyterian connectional courts; both are far removed from the true corruption, which is the popish hierarchy that set one man over the whole church. The clearest General Assembly remains the one no man convenes — the church of the firstborn, written in heaven, gathered unto mount Sion.
